# Welcome to indexing day!

Day 2, 10:15 · Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations · coverage: transcript, slides

Presented by Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin (named in the host's hand-over; turns not attributable). Highly rated Slido questions skipped on Day 1 for lack of time: four on slides with written answers, one more (sloppy migrations) only spoken, then a recap of Day 1. Transcript from a second attendee recording.

- **[Analysis]** Google's answer did not say whether HTML sitemaps pass link equity. On a large site, check that every important page is linked from a category or hub page in the normal navigation instead of relying on an HTML sitemap page to reach it.

- **[Docs]** Google's ecommerce documentation recommends linking from menus to category pages, from category pages to sub-category pages and from sub-category pages to all product pages; where not every product can be linked, it recommends a sitemap or a Merchant Center feed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C005` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Help Google understand your ecommerce website structure](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/ecommerce/help-google-understand-your-ecommerce-site-structure) · Used by `DEV-URL-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's ecommerce documentation says Google can infer a page's relative importance within a site from its internal links, such as how many links point to the page and how many links Google must follow to reach it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C006` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Help Google understand your ecommerce website structure](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/ecommerce/help-google-understand-your-ecommerce-site-structure) · Used by `DEV-URL-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** A 2005 Search Central blog post, now marked as possibly outdated, said Google encouraged HTML sitemaps because they help users navigate a site and a clear hierarchy of text links helps Google index it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C007` · Search Central blog (26 September 2005) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [How is a Google Sitemap different from an HTML sitemap?](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2005/09/how-is-google-sitemap-different-from)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's view of HTML sitemaps has moved: a 2005 blog post encouraged them, the current sitemap and ecommerce documentation does not mention them, and the 2026 Q&A slide pointed large sites to category hub pages instead.
  <br><sub>`D2-C008` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!</sub>

- **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C009` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (audience member) · Answered by [D2-C010](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C011](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C841](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

  - **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that whether to keep a temporarily out-of-stock product page or redirect it depends on how important that product page is to users.
    > "It depends on the importance of the PDPs to the users."
    <br><sub>`D2-C010` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C009](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C841](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-04`</sub>

  - **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide on out-of-stock product pages said users might wait months for some products, or even pre-order them if the site offers pre-ordering.
    <br><sub>`D2-C011` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Temporarily pause or disable a website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/pause-online-business) · Answers [D2-C009](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-04`</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Google contrasted out-of-stock products a buyer will wait for, such as a rare watch battery that matters to them, with easily replaced products, such as a particular cheese, for which the buyer simply picks a similar product instead of waiting.
    <br><sub>`D2-C841` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C009](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C010](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to temporarily pausing an online business recommends that a shop expecting to sell again within weeks or months stays online with limited functionality, such as a disabled cart, and updates its Product structured data to show current availability.
  <br><sub>`D2-C012` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Temporarily pause or disable a website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/pause-online-business) · Used by `DEV-ERR-04`, `DEV-SDA-08`, `DEV-SRV-03`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's redirect documentation says that with a temporary redirect, such as a 302, Google Search shows the source page in search results and does not use the redirect as a signal that the target should be canonical.
  <br><sub>`D2-C013` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Redirects and Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects) · Used by `DEV-CAN-01`, `DEV-ERR-04`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Keep a product page that is out of stock for a few months live with a 200 status, show its availability on the page and in Product structured data, and offer pre-ordering where possible when users would wait for the product. Redirect it only when users would rather switch to a similar product than wait.
  <br><sub>`D2-C014` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Used by `DEV-ERR-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
  <br><sub>`D2-C019` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (audience member) · Answered by [D2-C020](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C021](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C844](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C845](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C846](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

  - **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
    > "Simply put, it's because of sites that are extremely important and like to disallow their most important pages, either accidentally or out of ignorance."
    <br><sub>`D2-C020` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C019](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C110](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D2-C844](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

  - **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.
    <br><sub>`D2-C021` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [No page information in search results](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7489871?hl=en) · Answers [D2-C019](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C105](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D2-C846](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Repeated by [D2-C851](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Extended by [D2-C933](D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
    <br><sub>`D2-C844` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Answers [D2-C019](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C020](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Google said very few URLs disallowed by robots.txt are in its index, compared with the index as a whole (no figure given).
    <br><sub>`D2-C845` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C019](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
    > "if a URL is important, then it might get indexed even if it's disallowed by robots.txt. So the URL gets indexed, not the content."
    <br><sub>`D2-C846` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Answers [D2-C019](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C021](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C110](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's noindex documentation says the noindex rule works only if the page is not blocked by robots.txt: a crawler that cannot fetch the page never sees the rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C022` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Block Search indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) · Extends [D1-C106](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`, the glossary term *noindex*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Explain robots.txt and noindex to developers as two separate controls: robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing. To keep a page out of Search, let Google crawl it and serve noindex; a robots.txt disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C023` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's sitemap guide says Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently and verifiably accurate, and counts a change to the main content, the structured data or the links of a page as significant, but not a changed copyright date.
  <br><sub>`D2-C833` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Build and submit a sitemap](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap) · Used by `DEV-URL-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** An audience member asked how several sloppy migrations on the same domain can affect Googlebot's crawling.
  <br><sub>`D2-C839` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (audience member) · Answered by [D2-C840](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Google answered that several sloppy migrations on one domain can cause many effects in the short term, and noted that migrations concern indexing as well as crawling, a subject a later Day 2 talk would cover.
    <br><sub>`D2-C840` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [How to move a site](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes) · Answers [D2-C839](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Opening Day 2, Google recapped that Day 1 began with how Search works and then covered crawling, including basics of how the internet works such as TCP/IP, so that attendees could understand how crawlers work.
  <br><sub>`D2-C847` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · Repeats [D1-C317](D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said it strongly believes site owners should be able to opt out of crawling and control how their site is crawled, which can matter for legal reasons or for crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D2-C848` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Repeats [D1-C329](D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's robots.txt introduction names links from elsewhere on the web as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, while on stage Google spoke of the URL's importance; either way, well-linked important URLs are the disallowed ones most likely to appear in results, so keep such pages crawlable with noindex if they must stay out of Search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C849` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Extends [D1-C110](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>
